sections.text: The Regulation establishes rules for the protection of natural persons in relation to the processing of personal data and rules governing the free movement of personal data.
The Regulation protects the fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons, in particular their right to the protection of personal data.

The free movement of personal data within the Union must neither be restricted nor prohibited for reasons connected with the protection of natural persons in relation to the processing of personal data.

The Regulation applies to processing of personal data carried out wholly or partly by automated means, and to non-automated processing of personal data that forms part of, or is intended to form part of, a filing system.

The Regulation does not apply to processing of personal data in activities outside the scope of Union law; Member State activities within Chapter 2 of Title V TEU; purely personal or household activities by a natural person; or processing by competent authorities for preventing, investigating, detecting or prosecuting criminal offences, executing criminal penalties, or safeguarding against and preventing threats to public security.

Processing of personal data by Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies is subject to Regulation (EC) No 45/2001. That Regulation and other applicable Union legal acts must be adapted to the principles and rules of this Regulation in accordance with Article 98.
The Regulation does not affect the application of Directive 2000/31/EC, particularly its liability rules for intermediary service providers under Articles 12 to 15 of that Directive.

The Regulation applies to processing of personal data carried out in the context of the activities of an establishment of a controller or processor in the Union, regardless of whether the processing itself takes place within or outside the Union.

The Regulation applies to processing of personal data of data subjects in the Union by a controller or processor not established in the Union when the processing relates to offering goods or services to those data subjects in the Union, regardless of whether payment is required, or to monitoring their behaviour where that behaviour takes place within the Union.

The Regulation applies to processing of personal data by a controller not established in the Union where the controller is established in a place where Member State law applies by virtue of public international law.

‘Personal data’ means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person. A person is identifiable directly or indirectly, including through identifiers such as a name, identification number, location data, online identifier, or factors relating to their physical, physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural or social identity.

‘Processing’ means any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, whether automated or not, including collection, recording, organisation, structuring, storage, alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure, dissemination, combination, restriction, erasure or destruction.
‘Restriction of processing’ means marking stored personal data with the aim of limiting their processing in the future.

‘Profiling’ means any form of automated processing using personal data to evaluate personal aspects of a natural person, particularly to analyse or predict aspects such as performance at work, economic situation, health, preferences, interests, reliability, behaviour, location or movements.

‘Pseudonymisation’ means processing personal data so that they cannot be attributed to a specific data subject without additional information. The additional information must be kept separately and protected by appropriate technical and organisational measures.
‘Filing system’ means any structured set of personal data accessible according to specific criteria, whether centralised, decentralised or dispersed on a functional or geographical basis.

‘Controller’ means the natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body that, alone or jointly, determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. Where Union or Member State law determines these purposes and means, that law may also provide for the controller or specific criteria for its nomination.
‘Processor’ means a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body that processes personal data on behalf of the controller.

‘Recipient’ means a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body to which personal data are disclosed, whether or not it is a third party. Public authorities receiving data during a particular inquiry under Union or Member State law are not recipients, and their processing must comply with applicable data protection rules according to the processing purposes.

‘Third party’ means a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or body other than the data subject, controller, processor and persons authorised under the direct authority of the controller or processor to process personal data.

‘Consent’ means a freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication of the data subject’s wishes by which the data subject, through a statement or clear affirmative action, signifies agreement to the processing of personal data relating to them.

‘Personal data breach’ means a security breach resulting in the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss or alteration of, or unauthorised disclosure of or access to, personal data transmitted, stored or otherwise processed.

‘Genetic data’ means personal data relating to inherited or acquired genetic characteristics that provide unique information about a natural person’s physiology or health, resulting particularly from analysis of a biological sample from that person.

‘Biometric data’ means personal data resulting from specific technical processing relating to physical, physiological or behavioural characteristics that allow or confirm the unique identification of a natural person, such as facial images or dactyloscopic data.

‘Data concerning health’ means personal data related to the physical or mental health of a natural person, including the provision of health care services, where the data reveal information about the person’s health status.

‘Main establishment’ means the relevant central administration or establishment of a controller or processor in the Union determined under the conditions specified in this provision. For controllers, it is generally the central administration unless processing decisions are taken and implemented from another Union establishment; for processors, it is the central administration or, where none exists in the Union, the establishment where the main processing activities occur, insofar as specific GDPR obligations apply.

‘Representative’ means a natural or legal person established in the Union who is designated in writing by a controller or processor pursuant to Article 27 to represent them regarding their respective obligations under the Regulation.
‘Enterprise’ means a natural or legal person engaged in an economic activity, regardless of legal form, including partnerships or associations regularly engaged in an economic activity.
‘Group of undertakings’ means a controlling undertaking together with its controlled undertakings.

‘Binding corporate rules’ means personal data protection policies adhered to by a controller or processor established in a Member State for transfers or sets of transfers of personal data to a controller or processor in one or more third countries within a group of undertakings or enterprises engaged in a joint economic activity.
‘Supervisory authority’ means an independent public authority established by a Member State pursuant to Article 51.

‘Supervisory authority concerned’ means a supervisory authority concerned with processing because the controller or processor is established in its Member State, data subjects residing there are substantially affected or likely to be substantially affected, or a complaint has been lodged with that authority.

‘Cross-border processing’ means processing carried out in the context of activities of establishments in more than one Member State where the controller or processor is established in more than one Member State, or processing by a single Union establishment that substantially affects or is likely to substantially affect data subjects in more than one Member State.

‘Relevant and reasoned objection’ means an objection to a draft decision concerning an infringement of the Regulation or whether proposed action complies with it, which clearly demonstrates the significance of risks posed by the draft decision to data subjects’ fundamental rights and freedoms and, where applicable, the free flow of personal data within the Union.
‘Information society service’ means a service as defined in point (b) of Article 1(1) of Directive (EU) 2015/1535 of the European Parliament and of the Council.

‘International organisation’ means an organisation and its subordinate bodies governed by public international law, or another body established by or on the basis of an agreement between two or more countries.

article_name: Principles relating to processing of personal data

sections.text: Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently; collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not incompatibly further processed; limited to what is adequate, relevant and necessary; accurate and kept up to date; retained only as long as necessary, subject to permitted longer-term archiving, research or statistical processing under Article 89(1) with appropriate safeguards; and processed with appropriate security measures ensuring integrity and confidentiality.
The controller is responsible for compliance with the principles in paragraph 1 and must be able to demonstrate that compliance (‘accountability’).

Processing is lawful only where at least one legal basis applies: the data subject has given consent for one or more specific purposes; processing is necessary for a contract or pre-contractual steps; compliance with a legal obligation; protection of vital interests; performance of a public-interest task or exercise of official authority; or a controller or third party’s legitimate interests, unless overridden by the data subject’s interests or fundamental rights and freedoms requiring data protection, particularly for children. The legitimate-interests basis does not apply to public authorities performing their tasks.

Member States may maintain or introduce more specific provisions for processing based on Article 6(1)(c) or (e), including more precise processing requirements and measures to ensure lawful and fair processing in specific situations covered by Chapter IX.

The legal basis for processing under Article 6(1)(c) or (e) must be established by Union or applicable Member State law. That law must determine the processing purpose, or, for Article 6(1)(e), the processing must be necessary for a public-interest task or official authority. The legal basis may specify processing conditions, data types, data subjects, disclosures, purpose limitation, storage periods and processing procedures. The law must pursue a public-interest objective and be proportionate to the legitimate aim.

When further processing for a different purpose is not based on consent or a Union or Member State law under Article 23(1), the controller must assess compatibility with the original purpose by considering the relationship between purposes, collection context, nature of the personal data, possible consequences for data subjects, and appropriate safeguards such as encryption or pseudonymisation.
Where processing is based on consent, the controller must be able to demonstrate that the data subject has consented to the processing of their personal data.

Where consent is included in a written declaration concerning other matters, the request for consent must be clearly distinguishable, intelligible and easily accessible, using clear and plain language. Any part of the declaration that infringes the Regulation is not binding.

The data subject has the right to withdraw consent at any time. Withdrawal does not affect the lawfulness of processing carried out before withdrawal. The data subject must be informed of this before giving consent, and withdrawing consent must be as easy as giving it.

When assessing whether consent is freely given, particular account must be taken of whether a contract or service is made conditional on consent to processing personal data that is not necessary for performing that contract.

article_name: Conditions applicable to child's consent in relation to information society services

sections.text: For information society services offered directly to a child where Article 6(1)(a) applies, processing is lawful when the child is at least 16 years old. Below 16, processing is lawful only where consent is given or authorised by the holder of parental responsibility. Member States may set a lower age, but not below 13 years.
The controller must make reasonable efforts to verify that consent is given or authorised by the holder of parental responsibility, taking available technology into consideration.
Article 8(1) does not affect Member States’ general contract law concerning children, including rules on the validity, formation or effect of contracts.

article_name: Processing of special categories of personal data

sections.text: Processing of personal data revealing racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade union membership, genetic data, biometric data for uniquely identifying a natural person, health data, or data concerning sex life or sexual orientation is prohibited.

The prohibition in paragraph 1 does not apply where one of the specified exceptions applies, including explicit consent; employment, social security or social protection obligations and rights; protection of vital interests where consent cannot be given; qualifying activities of not-for-profit bodies; data manifestly made public by the data subject; legal claims or judicial activities; substantial public interest under Union or Member State law with appropriate safeguards; specified health or social care purposes; public health interests with safeguards; or qualifying archiving, scientific or historical research, or statistical purposes under Article 89(1).

Processing for the purposes referred to in Article 9(2)(h) is permitted where the data are processed by or under the responsibility of a professional subject to an obligation of professional secrecy under Union or Member State law or applicable rules, or by another person similarly subject to an obligation of secrecy.
Member States may maintain or introduce additional conditions or limitations concerning the processing of genetic data, biometric data or data concerning health.

article_name: Processing of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences

sections.text: Processing of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences or related security measures under Article 6(1) may be carried out only under the control of official authority or when authorised by Union or Member State law providing appropriate safeguards for data subjects’ rights and freedoms. Any comprehensive register of criminal convictions must be kept only under the control of official authority.

article_name: Processing which does not require identification

sections.text: Where the purposes for which a controller processes personal data do not or no longer require identification of the data subject by the controller, the controller is not required to maintain, acquire or process additional information to identify the data subject solely for the purpose of complying with the Regulation.

Where the controller is able to demonstrate that it is not in a position to identify the data subject, the controller must inform the data subject accordingly, if possible. In such cases, Articles 15 to 20 do not apply unless the data subject provides additional information enabling identification for the exercise of those rights.

article_name: Transparent information, communication and modalities for the exercise of the rights of the data subject

sections.text: The controller must take appropriate measures to provide information under Articles 13 and 14 and communications under Articles 15 to 22 and 34 in a concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language, particularly for information addressed to children. Information must generally be provided in writing or by other means, including electronic means where appropriate, and may be provided orally when requested if the data subject's identity is proven by other means.

The controller must facilitate the exercise of data subject rights under Articles 15 to 22. Where Article 11(2) applies, the controller must not refuse to act on a request unless it demonstrates that it is not in a position to identify the data subject.

The controller must provide information on action taken on a request under Articles 15 to 22 to the data subject without undue delay and in any event within one month of receiving the request. That period may be extended by two further months where necessary due to the complexity and number of requests, provided the data subject is informed of the extension and reasons within the first month.

Where the controller does not take action on the data subject's request, it must inform the data subject without delay and at the latest within one month of receipt of the request of the reasons for not taking action and of the possibility of lodging a complaint with a supervisory authority and seeking a judicial remedy.

Information provided under Articles 13 and 14 and communications and actions under Articles 15 to 22 and 34 must generally be provided free of charge. Where requests are manifestly unfounded or excessive, particularly because of their repetitive character, the controller may charge a reasonable fee or refuse to act, but must demonstrate the manifestly unfounded or excessive nature of the request.

Where the controller has reasonable doubts concerning the identity of a natural person making a request under Articles 15 to 21, the controller may request additional information necessary to confirm the identity of the data subject.

Information provided under Articles 13 and 14 may be presented together with standardised icons to provide a meaningful overview of the intended processing in an easily visible, intelligible and clearly legible form. Where the icons are presented electronically, they must be machine-readable.
The Commission may adopt delegated acts to determine information to be presented by standardised icons and procedures for providing standardised icons.

article_name: Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject

sections.text: Where personal data are collected from the data subject, the controller must provide information including its identity and contact details; the data protection officer's contact details where applicable; the purposes and legal basis of processing; the legitimate interests pursued where processing is based on Article 6(1)(f); the recipients or categories of recipients; and information concerning transfers to third countries or international organisations where applicable.

In addition to the information in paragraph 1, the controller must provide information necessary to ensure fair and transparent processing, including the storage period or criteria for determining it; the existence of rights of access, rectification, erasure, restriction, objection and data portability where applicable; the right to withdraw consent; the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority; whether provision of personal data is a statutory or contractual requirement and the consequences of failing to provide it; and information about automated decision-making, including profiling, where applicable.

Where the controller intends to further process personal data for a purpose other than that for which they were collected, the controller must provide the data subject with information about that other purpose and relevant additional information before carrying out the further processing.
Paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 do not apply where and to the extent that the data subject already has the information.

article_name: Information to be provided where personal data have not been obtained from the data subject

sections.text: Where personal data have not been obtained from the data subject, the controller must provide information including its identity and contact details; the data protection officer's contact details where applicable; the purposes and legal basis of processing; the categories of personal data concerned; the legitimate interests pursued where applicable; the recipients or categories of recipients; and information concerning transfers to third countries or international organisations where applicable.

The controller must also provide information necessary to ensure fair and transparent processing, including the storage period or criteria for determining it; the existence of rights of access, rectification, erasure, restriction, objection and data portability where applicable; the right to withdraw consent where processing is based on consent; the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority; the source from which the personal data originate and whether they came from publicly accessible sources; and information about automated decision-making, including profiling, where applicable.

The controller must provide the information within a reasonable period after obtaining the personal data, and at the latest within one month, taking into account the specific circumstances; if the personal data are used for communication with the data subject, at the latest at the time of the first communication; or if disclosure to another recipient is envisaged, at the latest when the data are first disclosed.

Where the controller intends to further process personal data for a purpose other than that for which they were obtained, the controller must provide information about that other purpose and relevant additional information before the further processing.

The information requirements do not apply where the data subject already has the information; where providing the information would involve disproportionate effort or prove impossible in specified circumstances and appropriate safeguards are applied; where obtaining or disclosure is expressly laid down by Union or Member State law; or where the personal data must remain confidential under a legal obligation of professional secrecy.

article_name: Right of access by the data subject

sections.text: The data subject has the right to obtain from the controller confirmation as to whether personal data concerning them are being processed and, where so, access to the personal data and information including the purposes of processing; categories of personal data; recipients or categories of recipients; the envisaged storage period or criteria for determining it; the right to request rectification, erasure, restriction or object to processing; the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority; the source of the data where not collected from the data subject; and information about automated decision-making, including profiling.

Where personal data are transferred to a third country or international organisation, the data subject has the right to be informed of the appropriate safeguards relating to the transfer under Article 46.

The controller must provide a copy of the personal data undergoing processing. For further copies requested by the data subject, the controller may charge a reasonable fee based on administrative costs. Where the request is made electronically, the information must generally be provided in a commonly used electronic form unless otherwise requested.
The right to obtain a copy must not adversely affect the rights and freedoms of others.

The data subject has the right to obtain from the controller without undue delay the rectification of inaccurate personal data concerning them. Taking into account the purposes of processing, the data subject has the right to have incomplete personal data completed, including by providing a supplementary statement.

article_name: Right to erasure ('right to be forgotten')

sections.text: The data subject has the right to obtain from the controller the erasure of personal data concerning them without undue delay, and the controller must erase personal data without undue delay where the data are no longer necessary for their original purposes; consent is withdrawn and no other legal ground exists; the data subject objects under Article 21(1) and there are no overriding legitimate grounds or objects under Article 21(2); the data were unlawfully processed; erasure is required by Union or Member State law; or the data were collected in relation to information society services offered to a child under Article 8(1).

Where the controller has made personal data public and is required to erase them under paragraph 1, the controller must, taking account of available technology and implementation cost, take reasonable steps, including technical measures, to inform controllers processing the personal data that the data subject has requested erasure of links to, or copies or replications of, those personal data.

The right to erasure does not apply where processing is necessary for exercising freedom of expression and information; compliance with a legal obligation; reasons of public interest in public health; archiving in the public interest, scientific or historical research or statistical purposes where erasure would render the purposes impossible or seriously impair them; or the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims.

The data subject has the right to obtain restriction of processing where the accuracy of personal data is contested, for a period enabling the controller to verify accuracy; processing is unlawful and the data subject opposes erasure and requests restriction instead; the controller no longer needs the personal data but the data subject requires them for legal claims; or the data subject has objected under Article 21(1) pending verification of whether the controller's legitimate grounds override those of the data subject.

Where processing has been restricted, the personal data may, except for storage, be processed only with the data subject's consent, for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims, for the protection of the rights of another natural or legal person, or for important public-interest reasons of the Union or a Member State.
A data subject who has obtained restriction of processing must be informed by the controller before the restriction is lifted.

article_name: Notification obligation regarding rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing

sections.text: The controller must communicate any rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing carried out under Articles 16, 17(1) and 18 to each recipient to whom the personal data have been disclosed, unless this proves impossible or involves disproportionate effort. The controller must inform the data subject about those recipients if the data subject requests it.

The data subject has the right to receive personal data concerning them that they have provided to a controller in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format and has the right to transmit those data to another controller without hindrance where processing is based on consent under Article 6(1)(a) or Article 9(2)(a), or on a contract under Article 6(1)(b), and processing is carried out by automated means.
In exercising the right to data portability, the data subject has the right to have the personal data transmitted directly from one controller to another where technically feasible.

The exercise of the right to data portability is without prejudice to Article 17 and does not apply to processing necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller.
The right to data portability must not adversely affect the rights and freedoms of others.

The data subject has the right to object, on grounds relating to their particular situation, at any time to processing of personal data concerning them based on Article 6(1)(e) or (f), including profiling based on those provisions. The controller must no longer process the personal data unless it demonstrates compelling legitimate grounds that override the interests, rights and freedoms of the data subject or the processing is necessary for legal claims.

Where personal data are processed for direct marketing purposes, the data subject has the right to object at any time to processing for such marketing, including profiling to the extent that it is related to direct marketing.
Where the data subject objects to processing for direct marketing purposes, the personal data must no longer be processed for those purposes.

At the latest at the time of the first communication with the data subject, the right to object under paragraphs 1 and 2 must be explicitly brought to the data subject's attention and presented clearly and separately from other information.

In the context of the use of information society services, and notwithstanding Directive 2002/58/EC, the data subject may exercise the right to object by automated means using technical specifications.

Where personal data are processed for scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes under Article 89(1), the data subject has the right to object on grounds relating to their particular situation unless the processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out for reasons of public interest.

The data subject has the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning them or similarly significantly affects them.

The prohibition in paragraph 1 does not apply where the decision is necessary for entering into or performing a contract; is authorised by Union or Member State law that also lays down suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights and freedoms and legitimate interests; or is based on the data subject's explicit consent.

In cases based on a contract or explicit consent, the controller must implement suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights and freedoms and legitimate interests, including at least the right to obtain human intervention, express their point of view and contest the decision.

Decisions under paragraph 2 must not be based on special categories of personal data under Article 9(1), unless Article 9(2)(a) or (g) applies and suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights and freedoms and legitimate interests are in place.

Union or Member State law may restrict, by legislative measure, the scope of obligations and rights under Articles 12 to 22 and 34 and Article 5 insofar as its provisions correspond to those rights and obligations, where the restriction respects the essence of fundamental rights and freedoms and is necessary and proportionate in a democratic society to safeguard specified objectives including national security, defence, public security, criminal-law enforcement, important public interests, judicial independence, prevention of ethics breaches, protection of data subjects or others, enforcement of civil law claims, and other important objectives.

Legislative measures restricting rights or obligations must contain specific provisions, where relevant, concerning the purposes of processing, categories of personal data, scope of restrictions, safeguards against abuse or unlawful access or transfer, specification of the controller or categories of controllers, storage periods and safeguards, risks to data subjects, and the right to be informed about the restriction unless that information could prejudice the purpose of the restriction.

Taking into account the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing and the risks of varying likelihood and severity to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller must implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure and demonstrate that processing is performed in accordance with the Regulation. Those measures must be reviewed and updated where necessary.
Where proportionate in relation to processing activities, the measures under paragraph 1 must include the implementation of appropriate data protection policies by the controller.

Adherence to approved codes of conduct under Article 40 or approved certification mechanisms under Article 42 may be used as an element to demonstrate compliance with the obligations of the controller.

article_name: Data protection by design and by default

sections.text: Taking into account the state of the art, implementation costs, and the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing and the risks to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller must implement appropriate technical and organisational measures, such as pseudonymisation, designed to implement data-protection principles effectively and integrate necessary safeguards into processing to meet the Regulation's requirements and protect data subjects' rights.

The controller must implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure that, by default, only personal data necessary for each specific processing purpose are processed. This applies to the amount of personal data collected, extent of processing, period of storage and accessibility, and measures must ensure that personal data are not made accessible to an indefinite number of natural persons without the individual's intervention.
An approved certification mechanism under Article 42 may be used as an element to demonstrate compliance with the requirements of this Article.

Where two or more controllers jointly determine the purposes and means of processing, they are joint controllers. They must determine their respective responsibilities for compliance with the Regulation, particularly regarding exercising data subject rights and providing information under Articles 13 and 14, through an arrangement between them, unless and to the extent their respective responsibilities are determined by Union or Member State law.
The arrangement must duly reflect the respective roles and relationships of the joint controllers vis-à-vis data subjects, and its essence must be made available to the data subject.
Irrespective of the terms of the arrangement, the data subject may exercise their rights under the Regulation in respect of and against each of the joint controllers.

article_name: Representatives of controllers or processors not established in the Union

sections.text: Where Article 3(2) applies, the controller or processor must designate in writing a representative in the Union.

The obligation to designate a representative does not apply to processing that is occasional, does not include large-scale processing of special categories of data under Article 9(1) or criminal-conviction and offence data under Article 10, is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, or to a public authority or body.

The representative must be established in one of the Member States where the data subjects whose personal data are processed in relation to offering goods or services, or whose behaviour is monitored, are located.

The representative must be mandated by the controller or processor to be addressed, in addition to or instead of the controller or processor, by supervisory authorities and data subjects on all issues related to processing for ensuring compliance with the Regulation.
The designation of a representative by the controller or processor is without prejudice to legal actions that may be initiated against the controller or processor themselves.

Where processing is carried out on behalf of a controller, the controller must use only processors providing sufficient guarantees to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures so that processing meets the Regulation's requirements and protects the rights of the data subject.

The processor must not engage another processor without prior specific or general written authorisation from the controller. Where general written authorisation is given, the processor must inform the controller of intended changes concerning the addition or replacement of other processors and provide an opportunity to object.

Processing by a processor must be governed by a contract or other legal act binding the processor to the controller and specifying the subject matter and duration of processing, nature and purpose, type of personal data, categories of data subjects, and controller obligations and rights. The contract must require processing only on documented instructions, confidentiality, appropriate security measures, assistance with data subject rights and compliance obligations, deletion or return of data after processing, and information and audit support.

Where a processor engages another processor to carry out specific processing activities on behalf of the controller, the same data protection obligations as those imposed on the initial processor must be imposed on the other processor through a contract or other legal act. Where the other processor fails to fulfil its obligations, the initial processor remains fully liable to the controller for that processor's performance.
Adherence by a processor to an approved code of conduct under Article 40 or an approved certification mechanism under Article 42 may be used as an element to demonstrate sufficient guarantees.

The contract or other legal act may be based, wholly or partly, on standard contractual clauses referred to in paragraphs 7 and 8, including where those clauses form part of a certification granted under Articles 42 and 43.
The Commission may lay down standard contractual clauses for the matters referred to in paragraphs 3 and 4 through implementing acts under the examination procedure referred to in Article 93(2).
A supervisory authority may adopt standard contractual clauses for the matters referred to in paragraphs 3 and 4 in accordance with the consistency mechanism referred to in Article 63.
The contract or other legal act referred to in paragraphs 3 and 4 must be in writing, including in electronic form.

Where a processor infringes the Regulation by determining the purposes and means of processing, the processor is considered a controller in respect of that processing, without prejudice to Articles 82, 83 and 84.

article_name: Processing under the authority of the controller or processor

sections.text: The processor and any person acting under the authority of the controller or processor who has access to personal data must not process those data except on instructions from the controller, unless required to do so by Union or Member State law.

Each controller and, where applicable, the controller's representative must maintain a record of processing activities under their responsibility. The record must contain the controller's and applicable joint controller's, representative's and data protection officer's contact details; purposes of processing; categories of data subjects and personal data; categories of recipients; applicable transfers to third countries or international organisations and related safeguards; and a general description of technical and organisational security measures under Article 32(1).

Each processor and, where applicable, the processor's representative must maintain a record of all categories of processing activities carried out on behalf of each controller. The record must contain the processor's and each controller's contact details; categories of processing carried out for each controller; applicable transfers to third countries or international organisations and related safeguards; and a general description of technical and organisational security measures under Article 32(1).
The records referred to in paragraphs 1 and 2 must be in writing, including in electronic form.
The controller, processor or representative must make the records available to the supervisory authority on request.

The obligations in paragraphs 1 and 2 do not apply to an enterprise or organisation employing fewer than 250 persons unless the processing it carries out is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects, is not occasional, or includes processing of special categories of data under Article 9(1) or criminal-conviction and offence data under Article 10.
Controllers and processors, including their representatives where applicable, must cooperate with the supervisory authority upon request in the performance of its tasks.

Controllers and processors must implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, taking into account the state of the art, implementation costs, processing characteristics, and the varying likelihood and severity of risks. Measures include, as appropriate, pseudonymisation and encryption, ensuring confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience, timely restoration of access and availability following incidents, and regular testing and evaluation of security measures.

When determining the appropriate level of security, particular account must be taken of risks arising from processing, including accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to personal data that is transmitted, stored, or otherwise processed.

Adherence to an approved code of conduct under Article 40 or an approved certification mechanism under Article 42 may be used as an element to demonstrate compliance with the security requirements in paragraph 1.

Controllers and processors must take steps to ensure that persons acting under their authority who have access to personal data do not process it except on the controller's instructions, unless Union or Member State law requires them to do so.

article_name: Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority

sections.text: Where a personal data breach occurs, the controller must notify the competent supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. If notification is made after 72 hours, the controller must provide reasons for the delay.
The processor must notify the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of a personal data breach.

A notification must at least describe the nature of the breach and, where possible, the categories and approximate numbers of affected data subjects and personal data records; provide the data protection officer's or other contact point's details; describe the likely consequences; and describe measures taken or proposed to address the breach and, where appropriate, mitigate its adverse effects.
Where the required information cannot all be provided at the same time, it may be supplied in phases without undue further delay.

The controller must document personal data breaches, including their facts, effects and remedial action taken. The documentation must enable the supervisory authority to verify compliance with Article 33.

article_name: Communication of a personal data breach to the data subject

sections.text: Where a personal data breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller must communicate the breach to the affected data subject without undue delay.

The communication to the data subject must describe the nature of the personal data breach in clear and plain language and include at least the information and measures specified in Article 33(3)(b), (c) and (d).

Communication is not required where appropriate technical and organisational protection measures were applied to the affected data, particularly measures such as encryption that make the data unintelligible to unauthorised persons; subsequent measures have ensured the high risk is no longer likely to materialise; or communication would involve disproportionate effort, in which case an equally effective public communication or similar measure must be used instead.

If the controller has not already communicated the breach, the supervisory authority may, after considering the likelihood of a high risk, require the controller to communicate it or determine that a condition in paragraph 3 is satisfied.

Where processing, particularly using new technologies, is likely to result in a high risk to natural persons' rights and freedoms, considering the processing's nature, scope, context, purposes and risk severity, the controller must conduct a data protection impact assessment before processing. A single assessment may cover similar processing operations presenting similar high risks.
The controller must seek the advice of the designated data protection officer, where one is designated, when carrying out a data protection impact assessment.

A data protection impact assessment is in particular required for systematic and extensive automated evaluation of personal aspects, including profiling, where decisions produce legal or similarly significant effects; large-scale processing of special categories of data under Article 9(1) or criminal-conviction and offence data under Article 10; or large-scale systematic monitoring of publicly accessible areas.

The supervisory authority must establish and publish a list of processing operations subject to the data protection impact assessment requirement under paragraph 1 and communicate those lists to the Board referred to in Article 68.
The supervisory authority may establish and publish a list of processing operations for which no data protection impact assessment is required and must communicate those lists to the Board.

Before adopting the lists under paragraphs 4 and 5, the competent supervisory authority must apply the Article 63 consistency mechanism where the lists concern processing related to offering goods or services or monitoring behaviour in several Member States, or may substantially affect the free movement of personal data within the Union.

The assessment must contain at least a systematic description of the envisaged processing and its purposes, including any applicable legitimate interest; an assessment of necessity and proportionality; an assessment of risks to data subjects' rights and freedoms; and measures addressing those risks, including safeguards, security measures and mechanisms for protecting personal data and demonstrating compliance while considering relevant rights and legitimate interests.

Compliance with approved codes of conduct under Article 40 by relevant controllers or processors must be taken into due account when assessing the impact of their processing operations, particularly for a data protection impact assessment.

Where appropriate, the controller must seek the views of data subjects or their representatives on the intended processing, without prejudice to protecting commercial or public interests or the security of processing operations.

Where processing under Article 6(1)(c) or (e) is governed by Union or Member State law, and a data protection impact assessment has already been carried out as part of a general impact assessment when that legal basis was adopted, paragraphs 1 to 7 do not apply unless Member States consider a further assessment necessary before processing.

Where necessary, the controller must review whether processing is performed in accordance with the data protection impact assessment, at least when the risk represented by the processing operations changes.

Where a data protection impact assessment indicates that processing would result in a high risk without measures to mitigate that risk, the controller must consult the supervisory authority before processing.

Where the supervisory authority considers the intended processing would infringe the Regulation, particularly because risks have been insufficiently identified or mitigated, it must provide written advice within up to eight weeks of receiving the consultation request and may exercise its Article 58 powers. The period may be extended by six weeks due to complexity, with notice and reasons, and may be suspended until requested information is obtained.

When consulting under paragraph 1, the controller must provide, where applicable, the responsibilities of the controller, joint controllers and processors; the purposes and means of processing; measures and safeguards protecting data subjects' rights and freedoms; the DPO's contact details; the Article 35 data protection impact assessment; and any other information requested by the supervisory authority.

Member States must consult the supervisory authority when preparing a legislative measure for adoption by a national parliament, or a regulatory measure based on such a legislative measure, where the measure relates to processing.

Member State law may require controllers to consult the supervisory authority and obtain prior authorisation for processing carried out in the public interest, including processing relating to social protection and public health, notwithstanding paragraph 1.

article_name: Designation of the data protection officer

sections.text: Controllers and processors must designate a data protection officer where processing is carried out by a public authority or body, except courts acting in their judicial capacity; where their core activities involve processing requiring regular and systematic large-scale monitoring of data subjects; or where their core activities involve large-scale processing of special categories of data under Article 9 or personal data concerning criminal convictions and offences under Article 10.
A group of undertakings may appoint a single data protection officer if that officer is easily accessible from each establishment.

Where the controller or processor is a public authority or body, a single data protection officer may be designated for several such authorities or bodies, taking their organisational structure and size into account.

In cases other than those in paragraph 1, controllers, processors, and associations or bodies representing categories of controllers or processors may designate a data protection officer, or must do so where required by Union or Member State law. The data protection officer may act for such associations and bodies.

The data protection officer must be designated based on professional qualities, particularly expert knowledge of data protection law and practices and the ability to perform the tasks referred to in Article 39.
The data protection officer may be a staff member of the controller or processor or may perform the tasks under a service contract.
The controller or processor must publish the data protection officer's contact details and communicate them to the supervisory authority.

article_name: Position of the data protection officer

sections.text: The controller and processor must ensure that the data protection officer is properly and timely involved in all issues relating to the protection of personal data.

The controller and processor must support the data protection officer in performing Article 39 tasks by providing the necessary resources, access to personal data and processing operations, and means to maintain expert knowledge.

The controller and processor must ensure that the data protection officer receives no instructions regarding the exercise of those tasks, is not dismissed or penalised for performing them, and reports directly to the highest management level of the controller or processor.
Data subjects may contact the data protection officer regarding all issues related to processing of their personal data and exercising their rights under the Regulation.
The data protection officer is bound by secrecy or confidentiality concerning the performance of their tasks, in accordance with Union or Member State law.
The data protection officer may perform other tasks and duties, but the controller or processor must ensure that those tasks and duties do not result in a conflict of interests.

article_name: Tasks of the data protection officer

sections.text: The data protection officer must at least inform and advise the controller, processor and relevant employees about their GDPR and other applicable Union or Member State data protection obligations; monitor compliance and related policies, responsibilities, awareness, training and audits; provide requested advice on data protection impact assessments and monitor their performance under Article 35; cooperate with the supervisory authority; and act as its contact point on processing matters, including Article 36 prior consultation, consulting where appropriate on other matters.
When performing these tasks, the data protection officer must have due regard to the risk associated with processing operations, taking into account their nature, scope, context and purposes.

Member States, supervisory authorities, the Board and the Commission are to encourage codes of conduct that contribute to proper application of the Regulation, taking account of different processing sectors and the specific needs of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises.

Associations and bodies representing controllers or processors may prepare, amend or extend codes of conduct specifying GDPR application, including matters such as fair and transparent processing, legitimate interests, data collection, pseudonymisation, information to the public and data subjects, data-subject rights, children's protection and consent, security and privacy measures, breach notification, international transfers, and dispute resolution.

Approved codes with Union-wide validity may also be adhered to by controllers or processors not subject to the Regulation under Article 3 to provide appropriate safeguards for transfers to third countries or international organisations under Article 46(2)(e). Such controllers or processors must make binding and enforceable commitments to apply those safeguards, including data-subject rights.

Codes of conduct must contain mechanisms enabling the body referred to in Article 41(1) to conduct mandatory monitoring of compliance by controllers or processors that undertake to apply the code, without prejudice to supervisory authorities' tasks and powers under Articles 55 and 56.

Associations and bodies intending to prepare, amend or extend a code must submit the draft to the competent supervisory authority. The authority must provide an opinion on compliance with the Regulation and approve the draft where it provides sufficient appropriate safeguards.

Where a draft code, amendment or extension is approved under paragraph 5 and does not concern processing activities in several Member States, the supervisory authority must register and publish the code.

Where a draft code concerns processing activities in several Member States, the competent supervisory authority must, before approval, submit it to the Board under the Article 63 procedure. The Board provides an opinion on whether it complies with the Regulation or, where paragraph 3 applies, provides appropriate safeguards.

Where the Board's opinion confirms that the draft code, amendment or extension complies with the Regulation or provides appropriate safeguards under paragraph 3, the Board must submit its opinion to the Commission.

The Commission may, by implementing acts, decide that an approved code, amendment or extension submitted under paragraph 8 has general validity within the Union. Such implementing acts must follow the examination procedure in Article 93(2).
The Commission must ensure appropriate publicity for approved codes that have been given general validity under paragraph 9.
The Board must collate all approved codes of conduct, amendments and extensions in a register and make them publicly available by appropriate means.

article_name: Monitoring of approved codes of conduct

sections.text: Monitoring compliance with an Article 40 code of conduct may be carried out by a body with appropriate expertise in the code's subject matter that is accredited by the competent supervisory authority, without prejudice to the authority's tasks and powers under Articles 57 and 58.

A monitoring body may be accredited where it demonstrates independence and expertise; establishes procedures to assess eligibility, monitor compliance and periodically review the code; establishes transparent procedures and structures for handling complaints about code infringements or implementation; and demonstrates that its tasks and duties do not create conflicts of interest.
The competent supervisory authority must submit draft accreditation requirements for monitoring bodies to the Board under the consistency mechanism referred to in Article 63.

Subject to appropriate safeguards and without prejudice to supervisory authorities' powers and Chapter VIII, an accredited monitoring body must take appropriate action where a controller or processor infringes the code, including suspension or exclusion from the code, and must inform the competent supervisory authority of the action and reasons.
The competent supervisory authority must revoke a monitoring body's accreditation where accreditation requirements are not or are no longer met, or where the body's actions infringe the Regulation.
The Article does not apply to processing carried out by public authorities and bodies.

Member States, supervisory authorities, the Board and the Commission are to encourage data protection certification mechanisms, seals and marks, particularly at Union level, to demonstrate compliance of controllers' and processors' processing operations with the Regulation, while taking account of the specific needs of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises.

Approved certification mechanisms, seals or marks may also demonstrate appropriate safeguards for transfers to third countries or international organisations by controllers or processors not subject to the Regulation under Article 3, where the transfer framework refers to Article 46(2)(f). Such controllers or processors must make binding and enforceable commitments to apply the safeguards, including those concerning data-subject rights.
Certification under this Article is voluntary and must be available through a transparent process.

Certification does not reduce the controller's or processor's responsibility for compliance with the Regulation and does not affect the tasks and powers of the competent supervisory authorities under Articles 55 and 56.

Certification must be issued by an Article 43 certification body or the competent supervisory authority, based on criteria approved by that authority under Article 58(3) or by the Board under Article 63. Board-approved criteria may result in a common certification known as the European Data Protection Seal.

A controller or processor submitting its processing for certification must provide the certification body or, where applicable, the competent supervisory authority with all information and access to processing activities necessary for the certification procedure.

Certification may be issued for a maximum of three years and renewed under the same conditions where the relevant criteria continue to be met. Certification must be withdrawn by the certification body or competent supervisory authority where the certification criteria are not or are no longer satisfied.
The Board must maintain a register of all certification mechanisms, data protection seals and marks and make them publicly available by appropriate means.

Certification bodies with appropriate data protection expertise may issue and renew certifications after informing the competent supervisory authority. Member States must ensure such bodies are accredited by the competent supervisory authority or national accreditation body in accordance with the specified accreditation standards and additional supervisory authority requirements.

Certification bodies may be accredited only where they demonstrate independence and expertise, undertake to respect the approved Article 42(5) certification criteria, establish procedures for issuing, reviewing and withdrawing certifications, maintain transparent complaint-handling procedures, and demonstrate that their tasks and duties do not create conflicts of interest.

Accreditation of certification bodies must be based on requirements approved by the competent supervisory authority or the Board. Where accreditation is conducted by a national accreditation body, those requirements must complement the applicable accreditation regulation and technical rules governing certification bodies.

Certification bodies are responsible for properly assessing certification and withdrawal, without affecting the controller's or processor's responsibility for GDPR compliance. Accreditation is issued for a maximum of five years and may be renewed where the certification body continues to meet the Article's requirements.
Certification bodies must provide the competent supervisory authorities with the reasons for granting or withdrawing requested certification.

The supervisory authority must make the accreditation requirements and Article 42(5) certification criteria publicly available in an easily accessible form and transmit those requirements and criteria to the Board.

The competent supervisory authority or national accreditation body must revoke a certification body's accreditation where the accreditation conditions are not or are no longer satisfied, or where the body's actions infringe the Regulation, without prejudice to Chapter VIII.
The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts under Article 92 to specify requirements to be taken into account for the data protection certification mechanisms referred to in Article 42(1).

The Commission may adopt implementing acts establishing technical standards for certification mechanisms, data protection seals and marks, and mechanisms for promoting and recognising them. Such implementing acts must follow the examination procedure under Article 93(2).

Transfers of personal data to a third country or international organisation, including onward transfers, may occur only where the conditions of Chapter V and the other provisions of the Regulation are complied with by the controller and processor. The Chapter V provisions must be applied so that the level of protection guaranteed by the Regulation for natural persons is not undermined.

article_name: Transfers on the basis of an adequacy decision

sections.text: Personal data may be transferred to a third country or international organisation where the Commission has decided that it, a territory or specified sector provides an adequate level of protection. Such transfers do not require specific authorisation.

When assessing adequacy, the Commission must consider factors including the rule of law, human rights, relevant legislation and its implementation, data protection and security rules, onward-transfer rules, case-law, enforceable data-subject rights and effective redress; independent supervisory authorities and their powers and functions; and the third country's or international organisation's international commitments and obligations concerning personal-data protection.

After assessing adequacy, the Commission may adopt an implementing act recognising a third country, territory, specified sector or international organisation as providing adequate protection. The decision must provide for periodic review at least every four years, specify territorial and sectoral application and, where applicable, relevant supervisory authorities, and follow the Article 93(2) examination procedure.

The Commission must continuously monitor developments in third countries and international organisations that could affect the functioning of adequacy decisions adopted under paragraph 3 and earlier decisions under Directive 95/46/EC.

Where information shows that adequate protection is no longer ensured, the Commission must, to the extent necessary, repeal, amend or suspend the adequacy decision without retroactive effect through implementing acts under the Article 93(2) procedure. On duly justified imperative grounds of urgency, immediately applicable implementing acts may be adopted under Article 93(3).
The Commission must consult the relevant third country or international organisation with a view to remedying the situation that led to the decision under paragraph 5.
A decision under paragraph 5 does not affect transfers to the relevant third country, territory, specified sector or international organisation that are carried out under Articles 46 to 49.

The Commission must publish in the Official Journal of the European Union and on its website a list of third countries, territories, specified sectors and international organisations for which adequate protection is or is no longer ensured.
Commission decisions adopted under Article 25(6) of Directive 95/46/EC remain in force until amended, replaced or repealed by a Commission decision under paragraph 3 or 5.

Where no Article 45(3) adequacy decision exists, a controller or processor may transfer personal data to a third country or international organisation only where appropriate safeguards are provided and enforceable data-subject rights and effective legal remedies are available.

Without specific supervisory authority authorisation, appropriate safeguards may be provided through legally binding and enforceable instruments between public authorities or bodies; Article 47 binding corporate rules; Commission-adopted standard data protection clauses; supervisory-authority standard clauses approved by the Commission; approved Article 40 codes of conduct with binding and enforceable commitments; or approved Article 42 certification mechanisms with such commitments.

With authorisation from the competent supervisory authority, appropriate safeguards may also be provided through contractual clauses between the relevant parties in the third country or international organisation, or provisions in administrative arrangements between public authorities or bodies that include enforceable and effective data-subject rights.
The supervisory authority must apply the consistency mechanism referred to in Article 63 in cases falling under paragraph 3.

Existing Member State or supervisory authority authorisations under Article 26(2) of Directive 95/46/EC remain valid until amended, replaced or repealed where necessary. Commission decisions under Article 26(4) of that Directive remain in force until similarly amended, replaced or repealed under paragraph 2.

The competent supervisory authority shall approve binding corporate rules under the Article 63 consistency mechanism where they are legally binding and enforceable throughout the relevant group, expressly confer enforceable rights on data subjects concerning their personal data, and meet the requirements of paragraph 2.

Binding corporate rules must specify at least the group's structure and contact details; covered transfers, personal data, processing, purposes, data subjects and third countries; their internal and external legally binding nature; application of general data protection principles and security and onward-transfer requirements; data-subject rights and remedies; liability for breaches by relevant non-EU members; how required information is provided to data subjects; DPO or compliance-monitoring responsibilities; complaint procedures; compliance verification, audits and corrective actions; mechanisms for reporting rule changes; cooperation with supervisory authorities; reporting third-country legal requirements that may adversely affect the rules' guarantees; and appropriate data protection training for personnel with permanent or regular access to personal data.

The Commission may specify the format and procedures for exchanging information between controllers, processors and supervisory authorities concerning binding corporate rules. Such implementing acts must follow the examination procedure under Article 93(2).

article_name: Transfers or disclosures not authorised by Union law

sections.text: A court or tribunal judgment or administrative authority decision of a third country requiring a controller or processor to transfer or disclose personal data may be recognised or enforced only when based on an international agreement, such as a mutual legal assistance treaty, between the requesting third country and the Union or a Member State, without prejudice to other transfer grounds under Chapter V.

Where no adequacy decision or appropriate safeguards exist, including binding corporate rules, transfers may occur only under specified derogations, including explicit informed consent, contractual necessity, contracts in the data subject's interest, important public interest, legal claims, vital interests where consent cannot be given, or certain transfers from public registers. Where none applies, a non-repetitive transfer involving only a limited number of data subjects may occur for compelling legitimate interests that are not overridden by the data subject's interests or rights, provided the controller assesses the circumstances, provides suitable safeguards, informs the supervisory authority, and informs the data subject of the transfer and compelling legitimate interests.

A transfer from a public register under paragraph 1(g) must not involve all personal data or entire categories of personal data contained in the register. Where the register is intended for persons with a legitimate interest, the transfer may occur only at their request or where they are the recipients.

The derogations concerning explicit consent, contractual necessity and certain compelling legitimate-interest transfers do not apply to activities carried out by public authorities in the exercise of their public powers.
The important public interest ground referred to in paragraph 1(d) must be recognised in Union law or in the law of the Member State to which the controller is subject.

Where no adequacy decision exists, Union or Member State law may, for important public interest reasons, expressly limit transfers of specific categories of personal data to a third country or international organisation. Member States must notify such provisions to the Commission.
The controller or processor must document the assessment and suitable safeguards relating to transfers under the second subparagraph of paragraph 1 in the records maintained under Article 30.

article_name: International cooperation for the protection of personal data

sections.text: In relation to third countries and international organisations, the Commission and supervisory authorities must take appropriate steps to develop international cooperation mechanisms; provide mutual assistance for enforcing personal data protection laws through notification, complaint referral, investigative assistance and information exchange with appropriate safeguards; engage relevant stakeholders in international cooperation activities; and promote the exchange and documentation of personal data protection legislation and practice, including jurisdictional conflicts with third countries.

Each Member State must establish one or more independent public authorities responsible for monitoring the application of the Regulation, protecting natural persons' fundamental rights and freedoms in relation to processing, and facilitating the free flow of personal data within the Union.

Each supervisory authority must contribute to the consistent application of the Regulation throughout the Union and must cooperate with other supervisory authorities and the Commission in accordance with Chapter VII.

Where a Member State establishes more than one supervisory authority, it must designate the authority representing them on the Board and establish a mechanism ensuring that the other authorities comply with the rules concerning the consistency mechanism under Article 63.
Each Member State must notify the Commission of the national legal provisions adopted under this Chapter by 25 May 2018 and, without delay, any subsequent amendments affecting those provisions.
Each supervisory authority must act with complete independence when performing its tasks and exercising its powers under the Regulation.

Members of supervisory authorities must remain free from direct or indirect external influence, and must neither seek nor accept instructions from anyone when performing their tasks and exercising their powers under the Regulation.
Members of supervisory authorities must avoid actions incompatible with their duties and may not, during their term of office, engage in any incompatible occupation, whether paid or unpaid.

Each Member State must provide its supervisory authorities with the human, technical and financial resources, premises and infrastructure necessary for effective performance of their tasks and powers, including mutual assistance, cooperation and participation in the Board.
Each Member State must ensure that each supervisory authority selects its own staff, who are subject exclusively to the direction of the supervisory authority's members.

Each Member State must ensure that each supervisory authority is subject to financial control that does not affect its independence and has separate, public annual budgets, which may form part of the overall state or national budget.

article_name: General conditions for the members of the supervisory authority

sections.text: Each Member State must provide for supervisory authority members to be appointed through a transparent procedure by its parliament, government, head of State, or an independent body entrusted with appointments under Member State law.

Each supervisory authority member must possess the qualifications, experience and skills required to perform their duties and exercise their powers, particularly in the area of personal data protection.
A member's duties end upon expiry of the term of office, resignation or compulsory retirement, in accordance with the applicable Member State law.
A member may be dismissed only for serious misconduct or where the member no longer fulfils the conditions required to perform the duties.

article_name: Rules on the establishment of the supervisory authority

sections.text: Each Member State must provide by law for the establishment of each supervisory authority; qualifications and eligibility conditions for members; appointment rules and procedures; terms of office lasting at least four years subject to the specified exception for the first appointment after 24 May 2016; reappointment eligibility and term limits; and conditions governing members' and staff's obligations, incompatible actions, occupations and benefits during and after office, and cessation of employment.

Members and staff of each supervisory authority must be subject to professional secrecy during and after their term of office regarding confidential information obtained while performing their tasks or exercising their powers, with the duty particularly applying during their term to reporting by natural persons of infringements of the Regulation.
Each supervisory authority is competent to perform the tasks assigned and exercise the powers conferred under the Regulation within the territory of its own Member State.

Where processing is carried out by public authorities or private bodies on the basis of Article 6(1)(c) or (e), the supervisory authority of the relevant Member State is competent, and Article 56 does not apply.
Supervisory authorities are not competent to supervise processing operations carried out by courts acting in their judicial capacity.

article_name: Competence of the lead supervisory authority

sections.text: For cross-border processing, the supervisory authority of the controller's or processor's main establishment or single establishment is competent to act as lead supervisory authority under the Article 60 procedure, without prejudice to Article 55.

By derogation, each supervisory authority may handle a complaint or possible infringement where the matter concerns only an establishment in its Member State or substantially affects data subjects only there.

Where paragraph 2 applies, the supervisory authority must inform the lead supervisory authority without delay. Within three weeks, the lead supervisory authority must decide whether to handle the case under Article 60, considering whether the controller or processor has an establishment in the Member State of the informing authority.

If the lead supervisory authority handles the case, Article 60 applies. The informing supervisory authority may submit a draft decision, which the lead supervisory authority must take utmost account of when preparing its draft decision under Article 60(3).
If the lead supervisory authority decides not to handle the case, the supervisory authority that informed it must handle the case in accordance with Articles 61 and 62.
The lead supervisory authority is the sole interlocutor of the controller or processor for that controller's or processor's cross-border processing.

Each supervisory authority must perform specified tasks within its territory, including monitoring and enforcing the Regulation; promoting awareness among the public, children, controllers and processors; advising public institutions; assisting data subjects; handling and investigating complaints; cooperating with other supervisory authorities; conducting investigations; monitoring relevant developments; adopting or approving contractual clauses, codes, certification criteria and binding corporate rules; maintaining relevant lists and records; conducting accreditation and certification activities; contributing to the Board; and performing other tasks related to personal data protection.

Each supervisory authority must facilitate the submission of complaints under paragraph 1(f), including through measures such as an electronically completable complaint form, while not excluding other means of communication.
The performance of the tasks of each supervisory authority must be free of charge for the data subject and, where applicable, for the data protection officer.

Where requests are manifestly unfounded or excessive, particularly because of their repetitive character, the supervisory authority may charge a reasonable fee based on administrative costs or refuse to act. The supervisory authority bears the burden of demonstrating that the request is manifestly unfounded or excessive.

Each supervisory authority has investigative powers including requiring information from controllers, processors and representatives; conducting data protection audits and certification reviews; notifying alleged infringements; obtaining access to personal data and necessary information; and accessing premises, processing equipment and means in accordance with applicable procedural law.
